text: Welcome everyone to today's special interview. I'm your host Rajesh Kumar, and we have an exclusive conversation lined-height businessman Vijay Mallya.
speaker: interviewer

text: Thank you for having me, Rajesh. It's always a pleasure to discuss business and life with an audience that cares about entrepreneurship.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: Let's start from the beginning. You built Kingfisher Airlines from nothing. What was that journey like in the early days?
speaker: interviewer

text: Kingfisher was a dream. We wanted to redefine aviation in India. Premium service, beautiful aircraft, and treating passengers like royalty. Those first flights in 2005 were magical.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: The audience is already applauding just hearing that. People remember those golden days fondly.
speaker: interviewer

text: Yes, and I laugh when I think about our launch party. We had champagne flowing and the whole team celebrating until dawn.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: Speaking of celebrations, there was a famous moment on this very show years ago. Do you remember the 101 rupees incident?
speaker: interviewer

text: Oh absolutely. That was quite a stunt. You pulled out exactly 101 rupees from your wallet and handed them to me on live television as a symbolic gesture.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: That's right. I wanted to make a point about starting small. Here, let me recreate it. Vijay Mallya, I'm giving you 101 rupees right now as a reminder that every empire starts with a single coin.
speaker: interviewer

text: He accepts the notes with a smile and tucks them into his jacket pocket. The studio audience erupts in laughter and applause.
speaker: narrator

text: I still have those 101 rupees framed in my office. It's the most valuable money I've ever received because of what it represents.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: Moving on to more serious matters. The bankruptcy proceedings in London were devastating for your reputation. How did you cope emotionally?
speaker: interviewer

text: It was the darkest period of my life. I cried alone many nights. The media painted me as a villain, but they never showed the human side of what I went through.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: That must have been incredibly painful. The audience can feel the weight of those words.
speaker: interviewer

text: When the court announced the verdict, I was shocked. Completely shocked. I didn't expect the banks to pursue it so aggressively after all our settlement discussions.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: Let's talk about the banks. The value of those loans. We're talking about nine thousand crore rupees. Nine thousand crore. Can you put that number in perspective?
speaker: interviewer

text: People throw around crore like it's nothing. Nine thousand crore represents thousands of jobs, hundreds of suppliers, and years of operational investment that kept India's aviation sector competitive.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: Critics say you diverted funds to Formula One and your personal lifestyle. What's your response to that accusation?
speaker: interviewer

text: I deny those allegations completely. Every transaction was documented and legal. Force India was a separate corporate entity with its own financing structure.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: You seem angry when that topic comes up. Is that frustration still raw?
speaker: interviewer

text: I'm not angry, I'm passionate. There's a difference. When you've built something with your bare hands and watch others tear it down with half-truths, passion is natural.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: Tell us about your time in London. What was daily life like during the extradition hearings?
speaker: interviewer

text: London became my prison without bars. I'd walk along the Thames every morning, nervous about what the day would bring. The legal team at Westminster was my only anchor.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: There was a moment outside the courthouse when protesters were shouting. You looked frightened. What was going through your mind?
speaker: interviewer

text: Fear, honestly. Pure fear. When a crowd turns on you, all the money in the world can't protect you from that feeling of vulnerability.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: The first time you mentioned Kingfisher Airlines in this interview was about the launch in 2005. But when did you actually conceive the idea?
speaker: interviewer

text: The idea came to me in 2003 during a flight to Geneva. I looked around at the shabby interiors of Indian carriers and thought, India deserves better. That was the seed.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: And the last time we'll touch on this topic today: any message for the employees who lost their jobs when Kingfisher collapsed?
speaker: interviewer

text: To every pilot, cabin crew member, and ground staff: I am sorry. Truly sorry. I think about you every day. You deserved better from me and from the system.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: Powerful words. The studio is completely silent. You can hear a pin drop.
speaker: interviewer

text: Let's lighten the mood. You were known for throwing legendary parties. What's the most extravagant celebration you ever hosted?
speaker: interviewer

text: My 60th birthday on Goa beach. Five hundred guests, fireworks over the Arabian Sea, and a performance by a Grammy-winning artist. It cost roughly fifty crore.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: Fifty crore for a birthday party! The audience is gasping. Some are laughing nervously.
speaker: interviewer

text: I know how it sounds. But that night wasn't about money. It was about bringing together friends from every continent. Joy was the only currency that mattered.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: When the interviewer asked about your UB Group earlier, you mentioned your father. Tell us about Vittal Mallya and the legacy he left you.
speaker: interviewer

text: My father was a giant. He built United Breweries from a single brewery in Bangalore. He taught me that business is about relationships, not transactions.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: He passed away when you were only twenty-seven. That must have been a tremendous shock for the family and the company.
speaker: interviewer

text: I was devastated. I cried for weeks. But he had prepared me. At his funeral, I promised to protect what he built and expand it beyond his wildest dreams.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: Around ten minutes into our conversation today, we touched on the airline's premium service. Can you describe what made Kingfisher First class special?
speaker: interviewer

text: Kingfisher First was a flying five-star hotel. Full flat beds, personal butlers, gourmet meals by Sanjeev Kapoor. Passengers would enter the plane and their stress would vanish.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: Sanjeev Kapoor! The celebrity chef. Did he personally design the menu?
speaker: interviewer

text: Absolutely. We flew him to Toulouse to meet with Airbus. He created forty dishes that rotated seasonally. The lamb biryani at thirty-five thousand feet was legendary.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: Now for something completely different. There are rumors about a secret meeting in Dubai. Did you meet with bank officials there?
speaker: interviewer

text: I will neither confirm nor deny specific meetings. What I can say is that I have always been willing to negotiate in good faith to resolve outstanding obligations.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: That's a politician's answer, Vijay. The people want transparency.
speaker: interviewer

text: And I want fairness. When SBI and PNB refuse to consider asset-backed settlements while simultaneously seizing my properties, transparency cuts both ways.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: You mentioned SBI and PNB. State Bank of India and Punjab National Bank were the largest creditors, correct?
speaker: interviewer

text: Correct. SBI alone had exposure of over sixteen hundred crore. PNB was close behind. Together they held the majority of the debt portfolio.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: Let's play a quick game. I'll say a word, you say the first thing that comes to mind. Ready? Bankruptcy.
speaker: interviewer

text: Pain.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: Kingfisher.
speaker: interviewer

text: Legacy.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: India.
speaker: interviewer

text: Home. I want to come home.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: That answer got emotional. You can see tears forming. The audience is completely silent again.
speaker: interviewer

text: I miss Mumbai. I miss the street food at Mohammed Ali Road. I miss watching cricket at Wankhede Stadium. London is exile, not home.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: Before we wrap up, I want to ask about the viral clip from this show. The moment you stood up and pointed at the camera. What triggered that?
speaker: interviewer

text: A reporter had published lies about my daughter. I stood up, pointed directly at the lens, and said leave my family out of this. That clip got ten million views.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: Ten million views! That's the strongest hook for a viral short if I've ever heard one.
speaker: interviewer

text: Social media amplifies moments. That was a father protecting his child. Nothing more, nothing less.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: One final question. If you could go back and change one decision, what would it be?
speaker: interviewer

text: I would never have acquired Air Deccan. The integration destroyed our balance sheet. It was the single worst decision of my career.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: Air Deccan acquisition. Noted. Ladies and gentlemen, please join me in thanking Vijay Mallya for this candid conversation.
speaker: interviewer

text: Thank you, Rajesh. And thank you to everyone watching. Remember, every empire starts with 101 rupees.
speaker: vijay_mallya

text: The audience gives a standing ovation. Some are cheering, a few are still booing from the bankruptcy section.
speaker: narrator
